A1.justification: Despite the changed title and format, both PDFs describe the same wildfire-evaluation study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original NetLogo simulations, trained-DNN experiments, metric sensitivity analyses and comparisons on the Next Day Wildfire Spread dataset, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v3 retains the original synthetic and real-world experimental results and adds perfect-predictor calibration and mismatched-training convergence results in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The NetLogo interaction rules, ConvLSTM-CA and Conv-CA architectures, BCE training, autoregressive forecasting and use of ECE remain. The revised theoretical treatment and additional controls do not establish a changed prediction algorithm or model.

E1.justification: Both evaluate synthetic forest-fire evolution and Next Day Wildfire Spread, retaining the stochasticity levels and forecasting tasks. Added calibration and convergence checks reuse existing data settings. Epidemic and rumor propagation remain discussion or future-work topics.

E2.justification: Recall is removed from the reported cross-S-Level, long-horizon and architecture-comparison plots: v2 Figures 6, 7 and 14 become v3 Figures 5, 6 and 13. MSE is also dropped from the sample-size convergence comparison. Some captions still mention removed panels. The five NDWS model comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds fixed training at S-Level 10 to the sample-size convergence evaluation and evaluates a perfect Statistic-GT predictor. Its written calibration definition also permits a representative bin probability, often the midpoint, whereas v2 specifies the mean forecast within each bin. Whether the implemented calculation changed is unstated; retained training splits and prediction windows are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds checks of perfect-predictor calibration and convergence under mismatched stochasticity levels in Appendices E.6 and E.4. It removes v2's cross-S-Level macrovariance boxplots and steady-state histogram, and reduces NDWS qualitative examples from five to two. The main architecture, long-horizon and overlap-stratified analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both use 1,000-realization Monte Carlo characterization, metric standard deviations and shaded convergence curves. No changed repeated-training scheme, seed reporting, confidence-interval definition or significance-testing procedure is specified. Additional curves do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: The NDWS tables are numerically identical: v2 Tables 3–4 become v3 Tables 1–2, retaining U-Net's AUC-PR of 0.3302 and AR-NCA's ECE of 0.0012. Retained main cross-S-Level heatmap values also match. New results include near-zero perfect-predictor ECE and mismatched-training convergence curves; several metric panels, supplementary distributions and qualitative examples are removed.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.4.1 adds a central necessary-condition argument based on estimating conditional positive frequencies and explains why ignored dependencies prevent calibration from being sufficient for process fidelity. v2 primarily motivates ECE through Brier decomposition without this argument. v3 also presents a binned calibration/refinement decomposition and corrects the written S-Level formula for the stated percentage convention.

C1.justification: The central proposal to evaluate stochastic-process fidelity using ECE remains. However, v3's abstract and introduction newly claim a formal necessary-condition result and explicitly state that low calibration error is not sufficient, qualifying v2's broader characterization of ECE. Statistic-GT itself already appears in v2.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's sample-size and discrimination caveats, v3 explicitly acknowledges that calibration ignores dependencies and cannot establish full process fidelity. It explains limited discrimination through the excluded refinement term, discusses heterogeneous agents and unobservable mixed stochasticity levels in real wildfire data, and identifies validation beyond wildfire as future work. These substantially qualify interpretation and applicability.

D1.justification: v3 Section 4.1 explicitly assigns 1,000 simulations and 700 training simulations to each S-Level and identifies the main ConvLSTM as single-layer. This clarifies existing experimental documentation rather than demonstrating larger datasets or changed architecture. Kernel sizes, temporal windows and loss remain documented as before.

R1.justification: v3 adds Blattenberger and Lad's calibration/refinement reference and Shi et al.'s ConvLSTM reference. It removes Stephenson et al., Jin et al. and Wainwright and Ellis, alongside shortening the corresponding decomposition, video-prediction and cosmology discussion. The broader wildfire and stochastic-evaluation positioning remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial main-text passages are rewritten. Evaluation theory becomes Section 3.4, wildfire literature moves into Appendix B, the macrovariance experiment moves to Appendix E.1, and discussion and conclusion are consolidated. Earlier supplementary sections E–H are reorganized under a unified Additional Results section.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the two-column main layout with a single-column format, introduces the conceptual Figure 1, redraws and condenses multiple plots, relocates existing figures to appendices and adds perfect-predictor plots. Several panels and case-study rows disappear. Captions for Figures 5 and 13 still reference absent Recall panels, creating presentation inconsistencies.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the evaluation target clearer and adds an important necessary-versus-sufficient qualification, supported by perfect-predictor and convergence checks. These provide a modest interpretive improvement over v2. The gain is limited because broad claims that ECE exclusively evaluates process fidelity remain, some comparative evidence is removed, and stale captions reduce consistency; the principal benchmark results are unchanged.
